scopeReview: CED FUN-6.D.3 rearrangements by polynomial long division and completing the square, combined with previously developed substitution/basic primitives. Linear-factor rational remainders come directly from division, not BC-only partial fractions. Positive quadratic denominators, retained cancelled-point domains and finite endpoints are checked. No trigonometric substitution or integration by parts is required.
varietyReview: Linear-divisor quotient and log remainder, cubic/quadratic remainder substitution, shifted/scaled arctangent, shifted definite bounds, cancelled polynomial ratio with retained domain, constant quotient and atan remainder, nonunit quadratic leading coefficient, numerator splitting, multiply-back division error analysis, higher-degree finite ratio and square-completion coefficient error analysis. Nine original-integrand/candidate computations and two exact algebra reviews.
repetitionReview: Each prompt and all four options were read separately; distinct tasks/contexts within this set. Cross-topic exact duplicates checked by validator. Semantic similarity and AP difficulty remain judgment calls, not proven by an automated score.

questions.independentReasoning: Multiply the quotient and divisor back to obtain x²+3x+2, then add remainder 3 to recover the original numerator. Independently differentiate the complete primitive and combine its terms over x+1. The logarithm remains real because x+1>0.
optionReview: This swaps the quotient constant and remainder coefficient.
This loses the remainder factor 3.
Division gives x+2+3/(x+1), which can be integrated term by term.
The numerator is not the derivative of that logarithm’s argument.

questions.independentReasoning: Differentiate x²/2−(1/2)ln(x²+1) to get x−x/(x²+1)=[x(x²+1)−x]/(x²+1)=x³/(x²+1). This exact recombination independently checks both the division remainder and chain coefficient. The denominator is always positive.
optionReview: This reverses the sign of the division remainder.
This omits the factor 1/2 in the logarithmic substitution.
This drops the polynomial quotient and uses the wrong remainder sign.
Division gives x−x/(x²+1), and the remaining log term needs factor 1/2.

questions.independentReasoning: Independently differentiate (1/2)arctan((x+3)/2): the derivative is (1/4)/[1+(x+3)²/4]=1/[(x+3)²+4]. Expanding that denominator recovers the original polynomial, verifying both the shift and scale.
optionReview: Completing the square gives (x+3)²+4, including a scale 2.
This is four times the required primitive.
This omits the outer factor 1/2.
This fails to scale the shifted input by 2.

questions.independentReasoning: Check the primitive derivative directly and independently note that the shifted interval is [−1,1], with an even reciprocal-quadratic integrand. Twice the known integral from 0 to 1 is π/2. Original-integrand quadrature corroborates the value.
optionReview: This counts only one endpoint contribution.
The shifted arctangent changes from −π/4 to +π/4.
This reverses the endpoint order.
This replaces the denominator by its minimum throughout the interval.

questions.independentReasoning: Differentiate the selected primitive to recover x+2, then multiply it by the original denominator to recover x²−4. The interval restriction is retained throughout. Numerical checks stay to the right of the cancelled point rather than assigning a value to the original ratio there.
optionReview: The ratio simplifies to a line, not a reciprocal.
This keeps the wrong sign after cancelling the common factor.
The original ratio equals x+2 on its allowed domain.
This is the simplified integrand, not its primitive.

questions.independentReasoning: Differentiate the proposed primitive: 1−1/[1+x²/4]=1−4/(x²+4)=x²/(x²+4). This independent simplification verifies the scale of the inverse tangent and the subtraction sign. All formulas are evaluated on a denominator-positive real domain.
optionReview: This loses a factor 2 in the integrated remainder.
This gives the wrong sign to the division remainder.
This omits the quotient and uses the opposite remainder contribution.
Division gives 1−4/(x²+4), with the scaled inverse-tangent remainder.

questions.independentReasoning: Differentiate (1/4)arctan(x+1/2) to obtain 1/[4(1+(x+1/2)²)]. Expansion of the denominator is 4x²+4x+5. This separately checks the leading coefficient, half-shift and residual constant.
optionReview: The denominator is 4[(x+1/2)²+1].
This is twice the required primitive.
This omits the denominator’s outer factor 4.
This changes the shifted input’s scale without compensating correctly.

questions.independentReasoning: Independently integrate the polynomial and reciprocal pieces over the same interval. The linear area is a trapezoid of width 1 and heights 1,2, giving 3/2; the reciprocal integral is ln 2. Original-ratio quadrature agrees with their sum.
optionReview: This omits the factor 1/2 in the polynomial primitive.
Division gives x+1/x, whose endpoint contributions are 3/2 and ln 2.
This incorrectly subtracts the reciprocal remainder contribution.
This drops the polynomial quotient.

questions.independentReasoning: Multiply the selected rewrite by x−2: (2x+3)(x−2)+10=2x²−x+4, exactly the original numerator. The first wrong rewrite yields 2x²−9x+4, and using remainder 4 yields constant −2. Changing the divisor also changes the excluded input and cannot be an equivalent formula.
optionReview: Multiplication gives the wrong linear coefficient.
This uses the numerator constant as the remainder without subtracting the quotient product.
Multiplying the quotient by x−2 leaves remainder 10.
This changes the original divisor and pole.

questions.independentReasoning: Multiply the quotient x²−x+1 by x+1 to get x³+1; the remainder −1 recovers x³. Differentiate the complete primitive independently and note the final value is positive, about 0.140186. Quadrature of the original ratio corroborates it.
optionReview: This reverses the remainder sign.
This omits the net contribution 1/3−1/2 of the higher polynomial powers.
The polynomial endpoint contribution is 5/6, not 1/6; this option also gives a negative value for a positive integrand.
Long division gives x²−x+1−1/(x+1).
